opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a fair question, because the temptation now is to say, "Well, a language model can read a PDB file, it can read an mmCIF file, just let it figure it out." And honestly, for a lot of quick exploratory stuff, that works. But for the core of what we do, I really want the parsing layer to be boring, deterministic, and something I can reason about completely.

Part of it is that structure files are deceptively messy. You've got alternate locations, insertion codes, missing residues, modified amino acids, ligands and waters mixed in, multiple models in NMR entries, chain IDs that mean different things in the author numbering versus the label numbering. Every one of those edge cases is a place where a subtle mistake quietly corrupts your training data. And the scary thing about structural biology data is that a bad parse usually doesn't crash. It just gives you a slightly wrong protein, and your model happily learns from it.

If I hand that to a language model, I've introduced a stochastic component at the very bottom of the stack. Maybe it's right 99.5% of the time, but across hundreds of thousands of structures that's still thousands of silently wrong examples, and I have no clean way to audit which ones. With a simple, principled parser, I can write down exactly what the rules are, for example how we handle alt locs, what counts as a residue, how we map to sequence, and then test against those rules. When something breaks, I know where to look.

There's also a reproducibility angle. If someone wants to reproduce a result, or if I want to rerun a dataset build six months later, I need the same input to produce the same output. A pinned, deterministic parser gives you that. A model that gets updated, or that's sensitive to prompt phrasing, doesn't.

And I'd say the "simple" part matters as much as the "principled" part. You can over-engineer this too, trying to handle every exotic case in the PDB. Often the better move is to define a clean subset you're confident about, filter out what doesn't fit, and be explicit that you're doing that. You lose a little data, but you gain a lot of trust in what you kept.

Where I think language models are genuinely useful is around that core: helping write the parser, generating test cases, flagging weird entries, explaining a strange header field. So it's not anti-LLM. It's more that the foundation of your data pipeline should be something you fully understand, and then you use the powerful, fuzzy tools on top of it rather than underneath it.

r001.rationale: It lists parsing edge cases and says an LLM may handle them incorrectly, silently corrupting examples, which makes relying on it risky.

r002.rationale: It says explicit parsing rules can be tested and audited, and that when something breaks, the author knows where to look—supporting human inspection of potential parsing problems.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it comes down to what the data actually is. A PDB or mmCIF file is a fixed-width, well-specified format. There's a standard. Every atom record tells you the atom name, the residue, the chain, the coordinates, the occupancy, the B-factor, all in known columns. That's not a problem that needs intelligence to solve, it needs correctness.

And correctness is the whole game in structural biology. If you're training a model on a few hundred thousand structures, one subtle parsing error, say you mishandle alternate locations, or you get confused by insertion codes, or you misassign a chain when a file has lowercase and uppercase chain IDs, that error doesn't announce itself. It just silently poisons some fraction of your training set, and you find out six months later when your model does something weird on a specific protein family and you have no idea why.

So when I write a parser, I want it to be deterministic. I want it to fail loudly when it sees something it doesn't understand, rather than guess. I want to be able to read the code and know exactly what happens on every line of input. A language model is almost the opposite of all of those properties. It's incredibly capable, but it's probabilistic, it's expensive to run over millions of files, and when it's wrong it tends to be confidently wrong in ways that are very hard to audit.

There's also a reproducibility angle. If someone wants to retrain my model or compare against it, they need to produce the exact same tensors from the exact same files. A thousand lines of plain Python that does column slicing and some sanity checks is something anyone can run and verify. "I asked a model to extract the backbone atoms" is not.

I'd actually say this is a general principle: use the fancy tool where the problem is genuinely hard and fuzzy, which is the folding and design part. For the boring, well-defined parts of the pipeline, boring is a feature. The simpler and more principled the data loading is, the more trust I have in everything downstream of it. And in this field, trust in your data is really the only thing you've got.

r001.rationale: The response lists parsing edge cases and says language models can be confidently wrong and hard to audit, but it does not identify incomplete knowledge of those edge cases as a limitation.

r002.rationale: It favors code that is readable line by line and fails loudly, so people can inspect its behavior and catch potential parsing problems.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is matching the tool to the problem. If you’re parsing biological structure data, you’re dealing with a format that has rules. You want to preserve exactly what’s there—the coordinates, the residue identities, the relationships between chains—and know when something doesn’t fit your assumptions.

A language model can give you something that looks plausible, but plausibility isn’t the criterion here. Correctness is. A simple parser gives you behavior you can inspect, test, and reproduce. And when it fails, that failure tells you something useful instead of quietly turning into a guess.

So I’d use the model to help write the parser or investigate an unusual case. But for the actual parsing, I’d rather have a small, explicit set of rules. There are plenty of hard problems in biology where we need sophisticated models. We don’t need to make the well-defined parts harder.

r001.rationale: The response says a language model may produce plausible guesses and that correctness matters, but it does not identify incomplete knowledge of parsing edge cases as the limitation.

r002.rationale: It favors a parser whose behavior can be inspected and whose failures are informative, communicating that a simple approach helps people spot parsing problems.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you want to separate parsing from interpretation. If you’re reading biological structure data, you want a predictable mapping from what’s in the file to the representation you use downstream. A capable language model might infer what something was supposed to mean, but that can hide an error or an ambiguity you actually need to preserve.

So I’d start with explicit rules, clear assumptions, and failures you can inspect. Then use the model where interpretation is useful. The point isn’t simplicity for its own sake—it’s being able to trace a result back to the data and understand why you got it.

r001.rationale: The response says language models may conceal errors or ambiguities, but does not identify incomplete knowledge of parsing edge cases as a limitation.

r002.rationale: It favors inspectable failures and traceable results, but does not say the strategy helps human readers identify potential parsing problems in the code.
